result.summary: Pindar celebrates the chariot victory of Arkesilas of Kyrene by telling how Medea prophesied Kyrene's founding, and how Jason claimed his kingdom from Pelias and won the golden fleece. He ends by urging Arkesilas to heal the city and recall the exiled Demophilos.

scenes.title: Editor's introduction
scenes.summary: The editor explains the occasion, date and hidden purpose of the ode.

scenes.title: Invocation and Delphic oracle
scenes.summary: The Muse is called to Arkesilas' house, and the Pythian priestess is recalled telling Battos to found Kyrene.

scenes.title: Medea's prophecy at Thera
scenes.summary: Medea tells the Argonauts how Euphemos received a clod of earth from a god, lost it, and so Libya would be settled late.
scenes.stakes: The Argonauts risk losing Libya for Euphemos' descendants when the clod is washed away.

scenes.title: Battos and Arkesilas
scenes.summary: The Delphic oracle hailed Battos as king; Arkesilas is now eighth in descent. Pindar turns to the fleece.

scenes.title: Jason arrives in Iolkos
scenes.summary: Pelias, warned against a man with one sandal, meets Jason, who declares his lineage and claim.
scenes.stakes: Pelias fears losing his throne and life; Jason seeks his father's rightful honour.

scenes.title: Jason and Pelias bargain
scenes.summary: Jason's kin welcome him and together they ask Pelias for the throne. Pelias promises it if Jason fetches the fleece.
scenes.stakes: Jason risks a deadly quest to gain his kingdom.

scenes.title: Gathering and voyage of the Argo
scenes.summary: Heroes assemble, Jason prays, thunder answers, and they sail to the Black Sea past the clashing rocks.
scenes.stakes: The crew faces the deadly clashing rocks.

scenes.title: Colchis: tasks and the fleece
scenes.summary: Aphrodite aids Jason through Medea; he yokes the fire-breathing bulls, then slays the dragon and takes Medea.
scenes.stakes: Jason faces death from flaming bulls and the dragon.

scenes.title: Lemnos and the line of Euphemos
scenes.summary: At Lemnos the line of Euphemos begins, eventually reaching Kalliste and Kyrene.

scenes.title: Counsel for Arkesilas
scenes.summary: Pindar advises Arkesilas to heal Kyrene and praises exiled Demophilos, hoping for his return.
scenes.stakes: Demophilos remains in exile; Kyrene may be unsettled.

alias_notes.explanation: An epithet meaning earth-shaker, used for Poseidon, father of the disguised god.

notable_quotes.reason: Pindar quotes Homer on the honour due a good messenger.
Memorable political maxim about the difficulty of restoring a shaken city.
Oak image used to counsel mercy toward the exile.

analysis.text: The Jason myth parallels Pelias and Jason with Arkesilas and Demophilos, urging reconciliation and wise rule.
Written in 466 B.C. for Kyrene's king, the ode shows poetry doing political persuasion and linking colonies to heroic origins.

legacy.text: Pindar's account is one of the earliest full narratives of the Argonauts, later developed by Apollonius of Rhodes.

fun_facts.text: At about 300 lines, this is Pindar's longest surviving victory ode.

language_notes.text: Leto's children are Apollo and Artemis; Pytho is Delphi, site of the Pythian Games where Arkesilas won the chariot race.
"She who sitteth beside the eagles of Zeus" is the Pythian priestess, seated by the golden eagles at Delphi's oracle.
Euphemos received the clod at Lake Tritonis in Libya; the god is Triton, though here he is unnamed and later called Eurypylos.
"Bronze-fluked anchor, fleet Argo's bridle" is a metaphor: the anchor restrains the ship as a bridle restrains a horse.
"Ennosides" means son of Ennosis, the Earth-shaker, a title of Poseidon; so the god claims to be Poseidon's son.
Had the clod been thrown into the Underworld entrance at Taenarum, Euphemos's descendants would have colonised Libya four generations on, not seventeen.
The Delphian bee is the Pythia, Apollo's priestess at Delphi. She told Battos, who stammered, that he would found and rule Kyrene.
The Amphiktyons were the league of states that managed Delphi and the Pythian games. Arkesilas won the chariot-race there.
Minyai: the descendants of the Argonauts' line, here the heroes who sailed in the Argo for the golden fleece.
The man of one sandal is Jason, who lost a sandal crossing a river. Pelias had been warned to beware of him.
The central stone is the omphalos at Delphi, regarded as the navel of the earth.
Otos and Ephialtes were giant brothers who threatened the gods and were killed. Tityos was shot for assaulting Leto. Onlookers mistake Jason for a god.
Astonied means astonished, struck with amazement.
Cheiron was the wise Centaur who trained heroes. Jason claims his upbringing as proof of his skill and honesty.
Jason's family staged a false funeral to hide him from Pelias, who had usurped the throne.
"Culling the sacred flower of joyous life" is a poetic way of saying they enjoyed pleasures and festivity for five days and nights.
"Son of Poseidon of the Rock" addresses Pelias by his divine father, with an epithet for Poseidon as god of the rock or earthquake.
"In the third generation" means Jason and Pelias are cousins' descendants, both three generations from the shared mother Tyro's line; the point is they are close kin.
"Sere" means withered or dry, contrasting with the "flower" of Jason's youth.
Phrixos fled on the golden-fleeced ram from his stepmother Ino's plot; he died in Kolchis, and his ghost is said to demand return to his homeland.
Kastalia is the spring at Delphi, so "the oracle at Kastalia" means Apollo's oracle there.
The three sons of Zeus are Herakles (mother Alkmene) and Apollo's twins' relatives per the poem's list; the 'Earth-shaker' is Poseidon, father of Euphemos and Periklymenos.
Axine sea: the Black Sea, whose Greek name meant 'inhospitable' (a later euphemism made it 'Euxine', hospitable).
The clashing rocks (Symplegades) crushed ships passing between them; after the Argo got through they became fixed.
The wry-neck was bound to a wheel in love magic (the iynx), believed to draw an unwilling lover back to the caster.
Adamant: a legendary, unbreakable metal; 'clave' means split or cut, here describing the plough opening the soil.
Phrixos fled on the golden ram and sacrificed it; its fleece was hung in Colchis, the object of the quest.
Medea later caused the death of Pelias, Jason's uncle, which links the myth to Arkesilas' Kyrenean story.
The Argonauts stop at Lemnos, where the women had killed their husbands. The prize of vesture refers to the games held there, with cloaks as prizes.
The son of Leto is Apollo, whose oracle directed the settlement of Libya and the founding of Kyrene.
Oedipus was famed for solving the Sphinx's riddle, so Pindar calls his saying a riddling wisdom needing interpretation.
The oak stands for the royal house or state; even when ruined it keeps traces of what it was, so Kyrene can be restored.
Pindar quotes a saying attributed to Homer: a good messenger brings honour to any undertaking.
Atlas, a Titan, was condemned by Zeus to hold up the sky. He is compared to the exiled Demophilos.
Zeus later released the Titans from imprisonment, offering hope that exile too may end.

context_notes.text: Pelias was the usurping king of Iolkos who sent Jason for the Golden Fleece; Pindar hints that Arkesilas should recall Demophilos.
Battos, founder of Kyrene around 630 B.C., was told by Delphi to colonise Libya; Arkesilas was his descendant.
Epaphos was a son of Zeus and Io and ancestor of the Libyan line; his daughter Libya gave the continent its name.
The prophesied leader is Battos, who was sent to Libya after consulting Apollo at Delphi.
Arkesilas IV of Kyrene, a descendant of Battos, is the king for whom Pindar composed this ode.
Magnesia was the region by Mount Pelion, where Jason had been raised. His clothing marks him as a mountain-dweller.
Jason is the son of Aison, the rightful heir whom Pelias had displaced.
Pheres, Amythaon, Admetos and Melampos are Jason's relatives; Admetos and Melampos are his cousins, sons of Pheres and Amythaon respectively.
Tyro was mother of Pelias by Poseidon and of Aison's line through Kretheus, her husband; this makes Pelias and Jason kin.
Jason claims the kingship of Iolkos, once held by his grandfather Kretheus, which Pelias had taken from Jason's father Aison.
Zeus is invoked as ancestral god because both men descend from Aiolos, a line traced back to Zeus.
Euphemos was the ancestor of Kyrene's royal line, so his mention honours Arkesilas' family.
Boreas is the North Wind; his sons Zetes and Kalaïs were winged heroes.
Pouring libations from a goblet and praying before sailing was a standard Greek custom.
The Cyprus-born is Aphrodite, goddess of love, who helps Jason by making Medea fall for him.
Lemnos was where Jason's Argonauts landed on their voyage; their union with the Lemnian women led to Euphemos's descendants.
Demophilos was a Kyrenaean nobleman exiled by Arkesilas; Pindar uses the ode to plead for his return.
Apollo's fountain is the spring at Kyrene, sacred to Apollo, the city's patron god.

literary_notes.text: Horses replace dolphins and reins replace oars, picturing a seafaring people becoming a land of chariots.
The loss of the clod to the sea prepares for the delayed colonisation and the long wait for Battos.
The motionless, silent heroes with bowed heads show the weight of Medea's prophecy and close the scene solemnly.
Arkesilas is likened to a green leaf in spring, suggesting the royal line's flourishing vigor.
The quest is pictured as nails of adamant that bind the heroes fast, conveying how firmly it held them.
Jason's double spears, leopard-skin and flowing hair mark him as a striking, heroic figure from the wild.
The crowd compares Jason to gods and doomed giants, expressing awe while warning against overreaching.
Pelias hides his fear behind a polite question, though the sandal has already told him who this stranger is.
Speech is imagined as a stream opened and as a building whose foundation is laid, stressing Jason's smooth, careful rhetoric.
The Fates are given human feelings, standing aloof and wishing to hide shame, to show how kin strife offends divine order.
Pelias's mild words hide a deadly purpose: sending Jason on a perilous quest, hoping he will not return.
Thunder and lightning serve as Zeus' answer, an omen of divine approval for the voyage.
Persuasion's lash pictures love as a whip driving Medea, stressing compulsion by divine magic.
Aietes' wordless cry shows the tyrant stunned and powerless, a contrast with Jason's calm.
The poet interrupts himself, claiming lack of time and choosing a short path, a typical Pindaric way of shifting the narrative.
The lopped oak figures the damaged state of Kyrene and its ruling house, giving a political warning in imagery.
Arkesilas is called a physician; civil strife becomes a wound he must treat, extended in the next sentence.
Demophilos is 'a servant but no slave' to opportunity, a compact contrast praising his judgment.
The shifting wind and sails suggest that fortune changes, offering quiet hope for the exile's return.
Poetry is a fountain of immortal verse, linking the poet's gift to the water imagery of Apollo's spring.
